thread.document:
Group members: Alex Cao, Will Cai, Fangzhou Zhao
https://182blue.vercel.app

Project Summary We built a static website that turns Special Participation A submissions (LLM evaluations on CS 182/282A homework) into a structured, searchable, and theme-aware directory. Instead of living in a linear Ed feed, submissions become something students can reliably study from and staff can efficiently review at scale.

What We Built (User-Facing Features)

Home page (overview + entry points) 

Dynamic stats (total submissions, unique authors, unique LLMs, homework coverage) computed from the dataset.

Quick-access tag clouds for Provider / LLM / Homework that deep-link into the Browse page.

“Recent submissions” preview to make the newest posts discoverable immediately.

Browse page (the scalable directory) 

Full-text search across title/author/model/provider/homework/content.

Filters for Provider / LLM / Homework with counts so users see what’s available before clicking.

Sort options (newest/oldest/most views/author/LLM) + pagination for large datasets.

Shareable URLs that preserve state (e.g. ?hw=HW9&provider=OpenAI&llm=GPT-4o, plus ?thread=ID to open a specific submission directly).

Quick View modal: open a submission, skim the writeup, and access attachments + extracted external links without leaving the page (reduces “open 20 tabs” review workflows).

Insights page (aggregation Ed doesn’t provide) 

Course-level charts: model distribution, provider distribution, homework distribution, and model-by-homework usage.

Homework breakdown table + a curated qualitative summary (“strengths/weaknesses” patterns seen in student reports) + practical recommendations for using LLMs responsibly.

Theme-aware chart rendering so visualizations stay readable in both light and dark.

Syllabus / Resources page (course hub) 

A week-by-week schedule table that consolidates lecture topics, slides, discussions, and homework materials into one navigable page.

Direct links to official artifacts (slides/solutions/code zips) so students can jump from “HW10 evaluations” → “HW10 resources” without searching Ed.

Theme + UI Polish (Light/Dark Done Right)

Automatic dark mode via system preference plus a manual toggle with persistence (so users can keep a consistent reading mode).

Smooth light ↔ dark transition animations for background/text/borders/shadows to avoid harsh flashes.

Insights charts also switch cleanly between light/dark versions (with a fade) so the page doesn’t “jump” on theme change.

Respects reduced-motion preferences to avoid forcing animation on users who opted out.

Data Pipeline (Makes The Site Reliable)

Converts downloaded Ed threads into structured site data (website/data.js), enabling consistent filtering/sorting and accurate charts.

Normalizes messy real-world labels (LLM name normalization + homework ID standardization) so “GPT 5.1 Thinking” vs “GPT-5.1 thinking” doesn’t fragment filters.

Extracts and surfaces high-value artifacts: 

Attachments (especially PDFs) and external share links (Claude/DeepSeek/Mistral/etc.) so reviewers can access the underlying evidence quickly.

Optional extraction of student profile links when present in posts.

Accessibility + Quality-of-Life

Skip link + visible focus styles for keyboard navigation.

Modal is keyboard-friendly (Escape to close, focus trap, focus restored on close).

Print styles for cleaner hard-copy review.

Static deployment model: no backend required, fast load, easy hosting.

Dataset Scale (Current Snapshot)

168 submissions from 167 authors

HW0–HW13 coverage (14 assignments)

30 unique LLM labels across 10 providers

134 submissions include PDFs/attachments

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>This is great! Could we just have have two options for filters --- First by homework number and second by LLM used. Right now there are too many options and it is a bit busy. Is it possible to organize this to be cleaner and more streamlined and easier to navigate? Are there summaries that can be gleaned or consistent insights? E.g. can you glean that particular LLMs struggle with particular types problems? Are there issues consistently across all LLMs? Any such work would be very interesting. This is of course not required, but would be very cool!!</paragraph></document>

comments.content: Thank you for the feedback! We made two sets of changes:Streamlined Filters (from your first suggestion):Simplified the browse page to only two main filters: Homework and LLMMoved Sort options under a collapsible "More" dropdownRemoved the Provider filter and "By Provider" section from the home pageAdded Analytics & Insights (from your second suggestion):The Insights page now automatically analyzes all student writeups using keyword heuristicsIt identifies common strengths (e.g., "Step-by-step derivations," "Strong linear algebra") and weaknesses (e.g., "Math mistakes," "Hallucination," "Needs reprompting") across all LLMsEach LLM now shows which themes apply to it specifically, with percentagesAll tables (Homework breakdown, Provider market share, LLM analysis) are now dynamically generated from the actual data rather than hardcodedThis addresses your question about gleaning patterns like "which LLMs struggle with particular problem types" — the theme analysis now surfaces these insights automatically!
comments.document:
Thank you for the feedback! We made two sets of changes:

Streamlined Filters (from your first suggestion):

Simplified the browse page to only two main filters: Homework and LLM

Moved Sort options under a collapsible "More" dropdown

Removed the Provider filter and "By Provider" section from the home page

Added Analytics & Insights (from your second suggestion):

The Insights page now automatically analyzes all student writeups using keyword heuristics

It identifies common strengths (e.g., "Step-by-step derivations," "Strong linear algebra") and weaknesses (e.g., "Math mistakes," "Hallucination," "Needs reprompting") across all LLMs

Each LLM now shows which themes apply to it specifically, with percentages

All tables (Homework breakdown, Provider market share, LLM analysis) are now dynamically generated from the actual data rather than hardcoded

This addresses your question about gleaning patterns like "which LLMs struggle with particular problem types" — the theme analysis now surfaces these insights automatically!
